1. Emission of Semen.
At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Udāyī had committed an offense of intentional emission of semen, which was unconfessed.
He informed the monks:
"Friends, I have committed one offense of intentional emission of semen, unconfessed. How should I proceed?"
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“In that case, monks, let the Saṅgha grant the monk Udāyī the trial period (mānatta) of six nights for one offense of intentional emission of semen, unconfessed.
And thus, monks, it should be granted:”

I requested of the Saṅgha a one-month probation for two offenses that had been concealed for two months.
The Saṅgha granted me a one-month probation for those two offenses concealed for two months.
While I was undergoing that probation, the sense of shame arose within me.
“What if I were to ask the Saṅgha for another month of probation for two offenses that were concealed for two months?
He asked the Saṅgha for another month of probation for two offenses that were concealed for two months.
The Saṅgha granted him another month of probation for two offenses that were concealed for two months.
In that case, monks, that monk must undergo probation for two months, counting from the previous period.
But here, monks, a monk commits two offenses entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa), both concealed for two months:
he knows one month [of concealment] and does not know the other month.
Thus he requests from the Saṅgha a probation for one month out of two months for two offenses concealed for two months, for that month which he recognizes.
The Saṅgha grants him a probation for one month out of two months for two offenses concealed for two months, for that month which he recognizes.
While he is undergoing probation, he recognizes the other month as well.
It occurs to him:
“I have committed two offenses entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa), concealed for two months;
I recognized one month [of concealment], and I did not recognize the other month.”
I requested of the Saṅgha a probation for one month for those two offenses concealed for two months—the month that I knew—out of those two months.
The Saṅgha granted me a probation for one month for those two offenses concealed for two months—the month that I knew.
While I was undergoing probation, I became aware of the other month as well.
‘What if I were to ask the Saṅgha for another month of probation for these two offenses, both concealed for two months?
He asks the Saṅgha for another month of probation for these two offenses, both concealed for two months.
The Saṅgha grants him another month of probation for these two offenses, both concealed for two months.
In that case, monks, that monk must undergo probation for two months, counting from the previous offense.
But here, monks, a monk commits two offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), both concealed for two months;
he remembers one month and does not remember the other month.
He requests from the Saṅgha a probation for one month out of two months’ concealment for two offenses, for that month which he remembers.
The Saṅgha grants him a probation for one month out of two months’ concealment for those two offenses, for that month which he remembers.
While he is on probation, he remembers the other month as well.
It occurs to him:
“I have committed two offenses entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa), concealed for two months;
for one month I remembered them, and for one month I did not remember them.”
I, having concealed two offenses for two months, requested from the Saṅgha probation for that month which I remembered.
The Saṅgha granted me probation for that month which I remembered out of those two offenses concealed for two months.
While I was on probation, I remembered the other month as well.
‘What if I were to ask the Saṅgha for another month of probation for these two offenses, both concealed for two months?
He asks the Saṅgha for another month of probation for these two offenses, both concealed for two months.
The Saṅgha grants him another month of probation for these two offenses, both concealed for two months.
In that case, monks, that monk must undergo probation for two months, counting from the previous offense.
But here, monks, a monk commits two offenses entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa), both concealed for two months:
for one month he is certain of his mind, and for one month he is uncertain.
Thus he requests from the Saṅgha a probation for one month out of two months for which he was unconscientious regarding two offenses concealed for two months.
The Saṅgha grants him a probation for that one month out of two months for which he was unconscientious regarding those two offenses concealed for two months.
While he is on probation, he becomes unconscientious regarding the other month as well.
It occurs to him:
"I have indeed committed two offenses entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa), concealed for two months:
for one month I was certain [of my offense], and for one month I was uncertain."
I, Saṅgha, requested probation for one month from among two offenses concealed for two months, for that month during which I was free from doubt.
The Saṅgha granted me probation for one month from among those two offenses concealed for two months, for that month during which I was free from doubt.
While I am undergoing probation, I have also been free from doubt regarding the other month.
‘What if I were to ask the Saṅgha for another month’s probation for these two offenses, each concealed for two months?
He asks the Saṅgha for another month’s probation for these two offenses, each concealed for two months.
The Saṅgha grants him another month’s probation for these two offenses, each concealed for two months.
In that case, monks, that monk must undergo probation for two months, counting from the previous period.
But here, monks, a monk commits two offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), both concealed for two months:
one month concealed knowingly, and one month concealed unknowingly.
He thus requests from the Saṅgha a two-month probation for two offenses concealed for two months.
The Saṅgha grants him a two-month probation for those two offenses concealed for two months.

While he is undergoing that probation, another monk arrives who is learned, of wide knowledge, a bearer of the Dhamma, a bearer of the Vinaya, a bearer of the Mātikā, wise, competent, intelligent, modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training.
Thus he speaks:
“Friends, what has this bhikkhu fallen into?
For what reason is this bhikkhu undergoing the period of probation?”
They speak thus:
“Friends, this bhikkhu has committed two offenses involving suspension (saṅghādisesa), concealed for two months:
one month was concealed knowingly, and one month was concealed unknowingly.”
He requested from the Saṅgha a two-month probation for two offenses concealed for two months.
The Saṅgha granted him a two-month probation for those two offenses concealed for two months.
"Friends, this bhikkhu has fallen into these [offenses], and this bhikkhu is currently undergoing probation for them."
Thus he says:
“Friends, this month which was concealed by the Saṅgha is a legitimate granting of probation for that month;
because it is legitimate, it takes effect.”
"And as for this month, friends, which was concealed without being known: the granting of probation for that month is unrighteous;
because it is unrighteous, it does not take root.
For one month, friends, a bhikkhu is worthy of the *mānatta* penance."
But here, monks, a monk commits two offenses entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa) that have been concealed for two months:
one month concealed while he remembers it, and one month concealed while he does not remember it.
He then requests from the Saṅgha a two-month probation for those two offenses, both of which were concealed for two months.
The Saṅgha grants him a two-month probation for those two offenses concealed for two months.

While he is undergoing that probation, another monk arrives who is learned, of wide knowledge, a bearer of the Dhamma, a bearer of the Vinaya, a bearer of the Mātikā, wise, competent, intelligent, modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training.
He speaks thus:
“Friends, what offense has this bhikkhu committed?
For what reason is this bhikkhu undergoing probation?
They replied thus:
"Friends, this bhikkhu committed two offenses entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa), both concealed for two months:
one month was concealed while he remembered it, and one month was concealed while he did not remember it.
He requested from the Saṅgha a two-month probation for those two offenses, both of which were concealed for two months."
The Saṅgha granted him a two-month probation for those two offenses concealed for two months.
"Friends, this bhikkhu has fallen into these [offenses], and this bhikkhu is currently undergoing probation for them.
He speaks thus:
“Friends, that month which was concealed while being remembered: for that month, the granting of probation is legitimate;
because it is legitimate, it takes root.
And that month, friends, which was concealed while not being remembered: for that month, the granting of probation is illegitimate.”
Because it is contrary to the Dhamma, it does not take effect.
"Friends, for one month, a bhikkhu is subject to the *mānatta* penance.
But here, monks, a bhikkhu commits two offenses involving formal meeting of the Sangha (*saṅghādisesa*), both concealed for two months.
One month was concealed with certainty of offense, and one month was concealed while being uncertain of the offense.
He requested from the Saṅgha a two-month probation for these two offenses, both of which had been concealed for two months.
The Saṅgha granted him a two-month probation for those two offenses, both of which had been concealed for two months.

While he is living there, another monk arrives who is learned, of wide knowledge, a bearer of the Dhamma, a bearer of the Vinaya, a bearer of the Mātikā, wise, competent, intelligent, modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training.
He speaks thus:
“Friend, what offense has this monk committed?”
‘Why is this bhikkhu undergoing probation?
They reply:
‘Friends, this bhikkhu committed two offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), both of which were concealed for two months.’
One month was concealed while he was free from doubt, and one month was concealed while he was under doubt.
He requested from the Saṅgha a two-month probation for two offenses that had been concealed for two months each.
The Saṅgha granted him a two-month probation for those two offenses that had been concealed for two months each.
"Friends, this monk has committed these [offenses], and for these he is undergoing probation.
He says this:
"Friends, as for that month which was concealed when there was no doubt, the granting of probation for that month is in accordance with the Dhamma."
Because it is in accordance with the Dhamma, it takes effect.
But this month, friends, which was concealed while being subject to doubt—that granting of probation for that month is un-Dhammic;
because it is not in accordance with the Dhamma, it does not take effect.
“Friends, for one month a bhikkhu is subject to the *mānatta* penance.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu had committed several offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (*saṅghādisesa*).
Thus, he does not know the limit of the offense;
he does not know the limit of the night.
He does not remember the limit of the offense; he does not remember the limit of the night.
He was uncertain as to the limit of the offense and uncertain as to the limit of the night.
He informed the monks:
"Friends, I have committed several offenses entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa)."
I do not know the limit of the offense, nor do I know the limit of the night;
I do not remember the limit of the offense, nor do I remember the limit of the night;
I am uncertain about the limit of the offense, and I am uncertain about the limit of the night.
“What, indeed, should I do?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“In that case, monks, let the Saṅgha grant that monk a *suddhanta-parivāsa* (probation until the end of purity) for those offenses.”
And furthermore, monks, it should be given in this way:
that monk, monks, having approached the Saṅgha...
[and so on] ...should speak thus:
“Venerable sir, I have committed several offenses entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
I do not know the limit of the offenses, nor do I know the limit of the nights [since they were committed];
I do not remember the limit of the offenses, nor do I remember the limit of the nights.”
‘I am in doubt as to the limit of the offense, and I am in doubt as to the limit of the night.
Venerable sir, I request the Saṅgha for purification through the end-of-the-purification (suddhantaparivāsa) for those offenses.
He should request it a second time as well.
A third time he should be requested.
A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me."
This monk named so-and-so has committed several offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa).
He does not know the limit of the offenses, nor does he know the limit of the nights;
he does not remember the limit of the offenses, nor does he remember the limit of the nights.
He is uncertain as to the limit of the offenses and uncertain as to the limit of the nights.
He requests from the Saṅgha a *suddhanta-parivāsa* (probation until the end of the purity) for those offenses.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant a *suddhanta-parivāsa* for those offenses to the monk named so-and-so.
This is the motion.
Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me.
This monk, named so-and-so, has committed several offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa).
He does not know the limit of the offense; he does not know the limit of the night.
He does not remember the limit of the offense; he does not remember the limit of the night.
He is doubtful regarding the limit of the offense; he is doubtful regarding the limit of the night.
Thus he requests from the Saṅgha purification through the end of the period of probation for those offenses.
The Saṅgha grants purification through the end of the period of probation for those offenses to the monk named so-and-so.
Whichever venerable one approves of granting purification through the end of the period of probation for those offenses to the monk named so-and-so, let him be silent.
Whoever does not approve of this, let him speak.
A second time I state this matter...
[as before] ...A third time I state this matter... [as before].
“The Saṅgha has granted such-and-such a monk the purification probation for those offenses.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I hold it.
In this way, monks, the purification probation should be granted.
In this way, the probation (parivāsa) should be granted.
And how, monks, is the probation of the pure end (suddhantaparivāsa) to be granted?
One does not know the limit of the offense, nor does one know the limit of the nights [spent in concealment].
If one does not remember the limit of the offense, nor does one remember the limit of the nights;
or if one is uncertain as to the limit of the offense, or uncertain as to the limit of the nights—
one should grant a *suddhantaparivāsa* (probation based on purity).
He knows the limit of the offense, but does not know the limit of the night;
he remembers the limit of the offense, but does not remember the limit of the night;
he is certain regarding the limit of the offense, but doubtful regarding the limit of the night.
A probation for the duration of the pure state (suddhantaparivāsa) should be granted.
[In this case], one knows some portion of the limit of the offense but does not know another portion; one does not know the limit of the nights.
One remembers some portion of the limit of the offense but does not remember another portion; one does not remember the limit of the nights.
If one is doubtful about the limit of the offense but not doubtful about the limit of the nights, or if one is doubtful about the limit of the nights—
one should be granted a *suddhanta-parivāsa*.
If one does not know the limit of the offense, but knows some of the limits of the nights and does not know others— one should be granted a *suddhanta-parivāsa*.
If he does not remember the limit of the offense but remembers some of the limit of the night and does not remember others;
or if he is uncertain about the limit of the offense but is certain about some of the limit of the night and uncertain about others—
a *suddhanta-parivāsa* (probation based on a clean confession) should be granted.
He knows the limit of the offense, but he knows some of the limit of the night and does not know others;
he remembers the limit of the offense, but he remembers some of the limit of the night and does not remember others;
he is certain regarding the limit of the offense, but he is doubtful regarding some of the limit of the night and certain regarding others.
A probation consisting of purification should be granted.
He knows some portion of the limit of the offense, but does not know another;
he knows some portion of the limit of the nights, but does not know another.
He remembers some of the limits of the offense and does not remember others;
he remembers some of the limits of the night and does not remember others;
regarding the limits of the offense, he is doubtful about some and free from doubt about others.
If, at the end of the night, he is doubtful about some [of the offenses] and certain about others,
a *suddhanta-parivāsa* (probation until the end of the offense) should be granted. This, monks, is how a *suddhanta-parivāsa* is to be granted.
And how, monks, should probation be granted?
One knows the limit of the offense and knows the limit of the nights;
one remembers the limit of the offense and remembers the limit of the nights.
One who is free from doubt regarding the limit of the offense, but is not free from doubt regarding the limit of the nights—
probation should be granted.
One who does not know the limit of the offense, but knows the limit of the nights...
If one does not remember the limit of the offense but remembers the limit of the night;
or if one is doubtful about the limit of the offense but certain about the limit of the night—
probation (parivāsa) should be granted.
He knows the limit of the offense in some cases and does not know it in others; he knows the limit of the night.
He remembers the limit of the offense in some cases and does not remember it in others; he remembers the limit of the night.
He is doubtful regarding the limit of the offense in some cases and free from doubt in others; he is free from doubt regarding the limit of the night.
The probation (parivāsa) should be granted.
This, monks, is how the probation is to be granted.
The probation is finished.
3. The Group of Forty:
Now at that time, a certain monk who was on probation left the Sangha.
Having returned again, he requested full ordination from the monks.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
"In this case, monks, a monk who is on probation disrobes.
For one who has disrobed, monks, the probation does not count."
If he is ordained again, his previous granting of probation remains the same.
That probation which was granted is well-granted; that which was undergone is well-undergone; the remainder must still be undergone.
But in this case, monks, a monk who is undergoing probation becomes a novice.
“Monks, probation does not take effect for a novice.
If he receives full ordination again, the previous granting of probation remains valid for him;
whatever probation was granted is well-granted, whatever was undergone is well-undergone, and the remainder must still be completed.”
But here, monks, a monk who is on probation becomes insane.
Monks, probation does not take effect for one who is insane.
If he later becomes no longer insane, that same original granting of probation applies to him.
The probation that was granted was well-granted; the probation that was undergone was well-undergone; the remainder must still be undergone.
But here, monks, a monk undergoing probation becomes deranged in mind.
Monks, for one who is deranged in mind, probation does not take effect.
If, however, he is again not distracted in mind, then for him that same previous granting of probation remains valid;
the probation that was granted is well-granted, and the probation that was undergone is well-undergone, though the remainder must still be spent.
But here, monks, a monk undergoing probation becomes overwhelmed by pain.
“Monks, for one who has undergone a change of feeling, the probation does not take effect.
If he becomes one who no longer has that change of feeling, then his previous granting of probation remains valid;
whatever probation was granted is well-granted, whatever was completed is well-completed, and the remainder must be spent.”
But here, monks, a monk who is undergoing probation may be suspended for not seeing an offense.
For one who has been suspended, monks, probation does not count.
If he is reinstated again, his previous granting of probation remains as it was.
The probation that was granted was well-granted; the probation that was undergone was well-undergone; the remainder must still be undergone.
But here, monks, a monk undergoing probation may be suspended for not making amends for an offense.
Monks, probation does not take effect for one who has been suspended.
If he is reintegrated again, his previous granting of probation remains as it was.
That probation which was granted is well-granted; that probation which was undergone is well-undergone; the remainder must still be undergone.
But here, monks, while a monk is undergoing probation, he is suspended for not relinquishing an evil view.
“Monks, the probation of one who has been suspended does not take effect.
If he is reinstated again, his previous granting of probation remains as it was;
whatever probation was granted was well-granted, whatever was undergone was well-undergone, and the remainder must still be completed.”
But here, monks, a monk who is deserving of being sent back to the beginning disrobes.
For one who has disrobed, monks, being sent back to the beginning does not take effect.
If he receives full ordination again, that same previous granting of the probation period applies to him.
The probation that was granted was well-granted; the probation that was undergone was well-undergone.
That bhikkhu should be sent back to the beginning.
Furthermore, monks, there is the case where a bhikkhu deserving to be sent back to the beginning is a novice... [and so on].
He becomes insane …pe… he becomes deranged …pe… he is overwhelmed by pain …pe…
He will be suspended for not seeing an offense...
he will be suspended for not making amends for an offense...
he will be suspended for not relinquishing an evil view.
“Monks, for one who has been suspended (*ukkhitaka*), the sending back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassanā*) does not take effect.
If he is reinstated (*osāriyyati*) again, then his previous granting of probation (*parivāsa*) remains exactly as it was:
whatever probation was granted is well-granted; whatever probation was undergone is well-undergone.”
That bhikkhu should be sent back to the beginning.
But here, monks, a bhikkhu who is deserving of the trial period (mānatta) disrobes.
For one who has disrobed, monks, the granting of the trial period does not take effect.
If he is ordained again, that same previous granting of probation remains valid for him;
the probation that was granted is well-granted, and the probation that was undergone is well-undergone.
That bhikkhu should be granted the *mānatta* penance.
But here, monks, a monk who deserves the *mānatta* penance is a novice (*sāmaṇera*) … he is insane … he is deranged … [and so on].
He is obsessed by feelings … [and so on] … he is suspended for not seeing an offense … [and so on] … he is suspended for not making amends for an offense … [and so on] …
If he is suspended for an evil view or for not relinquishing [that view], then,
monks, the granting of the *mānatta* penance does not apply to one who has been suspended.
If he is reinstated again, his previous granting of the *parivāsa* remains as it was.
The probation that was given was well given; the probation that was undergone was well undergone.
That bhikkhu should be granted the *mānatta* penance.
But here, monks, a bhikkhu who is practicing the *mānatta* penance disrobes.
“Monks, for one who has left the community, the practice of *mānatta* does not take root.
If he receives the full ordination (*upasampadā*) again, his previous granting of probation (*parivāsa*) remains exactly as it was:
whatever probation was granted is well-granted, and whatever was undergone is well-undergone.”
The *mānatta* that was granted was well-granted; the *mānatta* that was observed was well-observed; the remainder must be practiced.
But here, monks, while a monk is practicing *mānatta*, he becomes a novice (*sāmaṇera*) … or he becomes insane … [and so on].
He is deranged in mind …pe… he is overwhelmed by pain …pe… because of not seeing an offense, he is suspended …pe…
If one does not make amends for an offense, one shall be suspended; ...pe...
if one does not relinquish an evil view, one shall be suspended.
Monks, for one who has been suspended, the practice of the *mānatta* penance does not succeed.
If he is reintegrated again, his previous granting of probation remains as it was.
That probation which was granted is well-granted; that which was completed is well-completed.
That *mānatta* which was granted is well-granted; that *mānatta* which was practiced is well-practiced. The remainder must be observed.
But here, monks, a monk who is deserving of rehabilitation disrobes.
For one who has disrobed, monks, rehabilitation does not take effect.
If he should receive full ordination again, for him that same previous granting of the *parivāsa* period [is valid].
The probation that was granted was well-granted; the probation that was undergone was well-undergone.
The penance that was granted was well-granted; the penance that was practiced was well-practiced.
That bhikkhu is to be rehabilitated.
But here, monks, a novice monk is one deserving of rehabilitation … he is insane … he is deranged … [and so on].
He is distressed by his feelings … [and so on] … he is suspended for not seeing an offense … [and so on] … he is suspended for not making amends for an offense … [and so on].
If he is suspended for an evil view or for not relinquishing [that view],
monks, rehabilitation does not take effect for one who has been suspended.
If he is reinstated again, his previous granting of the *parivāsa* remains exactly as it was.
The probation that was granted was well-granted; the probation that was undergone was well-undergone.
The trial period (mānatta) that was granted was well-granted; the trial period that was practiced was well-practiced.
That bhikkhu is to be rehabilitated.
The Section of Forty is finished.
4. The Section of Thirty-Six.
Now, monks, here a monk who is undergoing probation commits several *saṅghādisesa* offenses in between, which are specified and unconfessed.
That bhikkhu should be sent back to the beginning.
But here, bhikkhus, while a bhikkhu is undergoing probation, he commits several *saṅghādisesa* offenses that are specified and concealed.
That bhikkhu should be sent back to the beginning.
And for those offenses of his that were concealed, a simultaneous probation (samodhānaparivāsa) must be granted for the previous offense.
But here, monks, if a monk who is on probation commits several *saṅghādisesa* offenses in the interim— whether some were concealed and some were unconcealed—
that monk must be sent back to the beginning.
And for those offenses of his that were concealed, a simultaneous probation (samodhānaparivāsa) should be granted for the previous offense.
But here, monks, while a monk is on probation, he commits numerous *saṅghādisesa* offenses: some immeasurable and unconcealed … [and so on] … some immeasurable and concealed … [and so on].
Immeasurable offenses, whether concealed or unconcealed … [and so on] … measurable or immeasurable offenses,
unconcealed … [and so on] … measurable or immeasurable offenses, concealed … [and so on].
Whether they were of limited duration or unlimited duration, concealed or unconcealed—
that bhikkhu should be sent back to the beginning.
And for his concealed offenses, a simultaneous probation (samodhānaparivāsa) should be granted in accordance with his previous offense.
But here, monks, a monk who deserves the *mānatta* penance...
[as above] ...while practicing the *mānatta* penance...
[the full passage should be expanded in the same manner as the *parivāsa*].
One deserving rehabilitation commits, in the interim, several *saṅghādisesa* offenses that are limited in number:
some unconfessed, some confessed, some both confessed and unconfessed... [and so on].
Innumerable unconcealed [offenses] …pe… innumerable concealed [offenses] …pe… innumerable both concealed and unconcealed [offenses] …pe…
Those that are limited as well as those that are unlimited,
whether unconcealed … [and so on] … those that are limited as well as those that are unlimited,
whether concealed … [and so on] … those that are both limited and unlimited, whether concealed or unconcealed.
That bhikkhu should be sent back to the beginning.
And for his concealed offenses, a probation concurrent with the previous offense should be granted.
The Section on the Thirty-six is finished.
5. The Hundred on the Trial Period (Mānatta-sata).
Now, monks, a monk here, having committed several offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), without concealing them, goes forth from the order.
Having been re-ordained, he does not conceal those offenses.
"Monks, that monk should be granted the *mānatta* penance.
Furthermore, monks, suppose a monk, having committed several offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (*saṅghādisesa*), goes forth into homelessness without concealing them.
Having been reordained, he then conceals those offenses."
“Monks, for that monk, having granted probation for the last category of offenses according to how long they were concealed, the trial period (mānatta) should then be granted.
But in this case, monks, a monk, having committed several offenses involving suspension (saṅghādisesa) and having concealed them, goes forth from the order.
Having been re-ordained, he does not conceal those offenses.”
"Monks, having granted that monk probation for the previous category of offenses as they were concealed, you must grant him the trial period (*mānatta*).
But here, monks, a monk, having committed several *saṅghādisesa* offenses and concealed them, goes forth from the community.
Having been re-ordained, he conceals those same offenses."
"Monks, for that monk, having granted probation for both the previous and the subsequent classes of offenses according as they were concealed, the *mānatta* (penance) should then be granted.
But here, monks, a monk commits several *saṅghādisesa* offenses.
His offenses are both concealed and unconcealed."
Thus, having disrobed and being ordained again, he does not conceal those offenses which he previously concealed,
